title: Đào tạo nghề và quyền lựa chọn · Problems / Solutions
prompt: Some societies are considering placing more school leavers in vocational training rather than university. What problems could this create, and what measures could be taken to address them?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

outline.purpose: Đề yêu cầu những vấn đề chính sách có thể tạo ra và biện pháp xử lý. grammar.pattern: if + mệnh đề điều kiện, mệnh đề kết quả

grammar.why: Điều kiện trong câu giới hạn kết quả theo hoàn cảnh được nêu; không được bỏ điều kiện rồi coi hệ quả luôn xảy ra. Không kết luận học nghề tốt hơn đại học cho mọi học sinh. Sở thích thực hành có thể đổi; nghề cụ thể cũng có thể mất nhu cầu. Ví dụ thợ điện minh họa một lộ trình, không xếp hạng mọi ngành học.

paragraphs: Moving more school leavers into vocational training risks locking students into an early choice when their qualifications do not provide entry to later university study. These risks call for genuine transfer pathways and clear information before enrolment, so a practical route remains a choice that students can later revise.

Early tracking can close academic opportunities before a young person's interests have matured. A teenager's initial route may determine which subjects and qualifications remain available later. If switching requires repeating years of study or meeting inaccessible entry requirements, an early practical preference can become a lasting restriction rather than a freely revisable choice. The case is strongest where placements teach transferable skills and lead to genuine vacancies, rather than simply supplying employers with cheap temporary labour.

Vocational qualifications should offer credible routes into further academic study. Colleges and universities should agree which vocational credits count towards admission, with bridging courses for the academic subjects a trainee has not yet studied. Transfer routes should recognise vocational learning and set achievable entry requirements, so a practical choice at sixteen does not become an irreversible academic exclusion. Published transfer requirements would let applicants compare future options before enrolling, rather than discover after several years that changing direction means starting again. Advisers should explain the time and cost of transferring as well as formal eligibility, because a theoretical route offers little protection if repeating years makes it unaffordable. A vocational system should be assessed both by employment outcomes and by whether students retain a realistic route into further academic study.
A stronger vocational sector deserves priority as an additional route to secure work, with success depending on both the skills acquired and the freedom to change direction.
